steps.text: Part 3 of 5: Your first moves: three habits. This part covers Knights before bishops; Why castle; Black's side. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Knights before bishops** is a common default, with a reason. [I] A knight's good squares, such as f3 and c3, are clear early whatever your opponent does. A bishop's best diagonal depends on where the pawns end up, so it often pays to wait and see. In the next board the bishop has several plausible squares, and one reply with a pawn changes the question at once.

steps.caption: White's bishop can go to b5, c4 or e2, and Black's pawns decide which is best. After the bishop goes to b5, one pawn move asks it a question straight away.

line.say: The bishop attacks the knight that guards e5.
A pawn asks the bishop what it wants to do. The pawns have changed the question.

steps.text: The queen is strong, so it is tempting to send it out early. [I] A queen out alone often gets chased by smaller pieces, and each chase can cost you a move. An early queen is not refuted by force, though: it works if Black ignores the threat. The next boards show the chase, and then what happens when Black does ignore it.

steps.caption: White's queen moved twice. Black developed two knights, and a pawn push gained a tempo by attacking the queen. [I] Black is simply ahead in development. Queen to h5 is not refuted: it works only if Black ignores the threat.

line.say: White opens.
Black copies.
The queen comes out and eyes e5 and f7.
Black guards e5 and develops.
The bishop joins the queen against f7.
A pawn attacks the queen with tempo.
The queen retreats and still eyes f7. White has used the queen twice.
The knight develops and shuts the queen's line to f7.

steps.caption: White's queen and bishop both aim at the pawn on f7. Black has just developed a knight and ignored them.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn, protected by the bishop. The king cannot capture it and has no square: checkmate.

steps.caption: Black to move. Several moves hold: attack the queen (g6), or add a guard to f7 (Qe7, Nh6, Qf6). [V] Checked at depth 16.

line.say: A pawn attacks the queen, so White must move it.
The queen retreats and still aims at f7.
Now the knight develops and blocks the queen's line to f7.

steps.text: Habit three: **castle**. Castling is one move that does two jobs: the king goes two squares toward a corner, behind its pawn shelter, and the rook leaves the corner for the middle. It is allowed only if neither piece has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check and does not cross or land on an attacked square. Castling toward the queen is slower [I].

steps.caption: White's knight is out but the bishop is still on f1, between the king and the rook.

line.say: The bishop leaves, so one blocker between king and rook is gone.
Black develops a bishop too.

steps.caption: Both squares between king and rook are empty now.

line.say: The king hops two squares to the corner and the rook lands next to it, closer to the centre files.

steps.text: The king hides best behind its pawns, but every pawn move in front of it is permanent and can open lines for enemy pieces. Before the next board, see if you can find the fastest checkmate there is. It works only because White moved the two pawns in front of its own king.

steps.caption: After 1.f3 e5 2.g4, Black plays Qh4 and it is checkmate.

line.say: The queen slides along the long diagonal and gives check. No piece can block or capture, and the king has no square.

steps.text: A king left in the middle is a target. In the next board Black has one piece out, the king is still on e8, and a bishop sacrifice has dragged it onto e7. A castled king sits behind three pawns, as in the model game later, and enemy pieces have to get past them first.

steps.caption: Black's king never castled and its pieces are undeveloped. The knight from c3 delivers checkmate. This is a well-known trap, usually called the Legal trap [R].

line.say: Checkmate: the knight on d5 gives check, and the bishop on f7 and knight on e5 cover every square.

steps.text: The same three habits work for Black; the pawns just point the other way. Against a queen-pawn start Black can answer with a centre pawn of its own, then develop knight and bishop, then castle. Against the king-pawn start Black often fights for the centre from the side with a c-pawn, which is the same habit seen from a distance [I]. The next board follows one calm Black game.

steps.caption: One calm game from Black's side: a centre pawn, a pawn to support it, a knight, a bishop, and castling.

line.say: Habit one: a centre pawn answers White's centre pawn.
White offers a pawn to pull the d-pawn away.
Black supports the pawn and opens the bishop on f8.
White develops a knight.
A knight comes out and watches the centre.
White pins the knight against the queen.
Black develops the bishop and unpins.
White opens the bishop on f1.
Habit three: Black castles.
